A little clarity changes everything

“It failed” is
only the beginning.

Your agent made a wrong call. The answer is somewhere in its tools, memory, and decisions. SuperTuriya brings those pieces together, then helps you test the smallest useful change.

Built for engineers who want to understand a failure before they let an agent learn from it.

The mechanism works.

SuperTuriya11 / 12

External-v2 · 16 blinded cases

Generalization is the next step.

Both systems recovered 8 of 16 cases. Strong diagnosis did not translate into a recovery advantage.

Direct baseline8 / 16
SuperTuriya8 / 16

Three recorded trials on AI-authored cloud-operations scenarios. Zero recovery lift is preserved in the evidence.

These results describe the evaluated versions. New repair-selection capabilities need their own evaluation. A passing replay is evidence within its captured environment and checks.

A few good questions

Let's make it clear.

What does SuperTuriya actually do?

It helps inspect a failed, stateful agent run, identify an evidence-backed diagnosis, propose a typed repair, and verify a replay. The local operator workflow requires human review before replay and separate review before activating a verified policy.

Can I connect my production agent today?

The repository provides trace APIs and a local deterministic control plane. A complete production integration, framework adapter, and customer validation remain in development. We are looking for a tightly scoped design-partner workflow.

Is the playground running an AI model?

No. It walks through recorded synthetic cases generated by the Python engine and deterministic verifier. Your clicks explore approval, evidence, and activation states locally. The repository includes an optional model-backed research path.

What happens when a repair is not good enough?

It stays blocked. Try the multi-causal case: correcting execution order still leaves evidence missing. The checks catch that remaining failure and prevent activation in the demo.

Is SuperTuriya open source?

Yes. The Python reference implementation is MIT licensed. You can inspect the source, run the local console, and reproduce the frozen evidence. The field guide explains the boundaries between the public playground and the operator runtime.
